subChunks.title: Design Tokens
subChunks.hookHtml: Out of the box, Tailwind's palette is named by colour — blue-500, purple-700. In a real product you need names by intent: brand, surface, danger. That shift is what separates a hobby project from a system that can survive a rebrand.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Archmage's library is colder than the rest of the tower. Scrolls line the shelves in perfect alphabetical order. Solomon doesn't look up when you enter — he is marking a token page with a silver nib.

Archmage Solomon: “At scale, blue-500 is a lie. It claims the colour is blue when what you mean is: this is the brand. Name by meaning. Then when the brand changes — and it will — your code does not.”

He slides a parchment across the table. It is a tailwind.config.js.

// tailwind.config.js
module.exports = {
  theme: {
    extend: {
      colors: {
        brand:   { DEFAULT: '#6D28D9', light: '#A78BFA', dark: '#4C1D95' },
        surface: 'var(--surface)',
        text:    'var(--text)',
        danger:  '#DC2626',
      },
      fontFamily: { display: ['Cinzel', 'serif'] },
      spacing:    { '18': '4.5rem' },
    },
  },
};

Solomon: “Once this is in place, bg-brand, text-brand-light, bg-surface, and font-display all become first-class utilities.”

He taps the parchment and lists the three token layers every serious system uses.

  1. Primitive tokens — raw values. purple-700, 4rem, 14px.
  2. Semantic tokens — intent. brand, surface, danger, text-muted.
  3. Component tokens — per-component overrides. Use sparingly.

Solomon: “The rule is simple. A <Button> component should never reach for a primitive. It should ask for brand, or danger, and trust the tokens to resolve to something sensible.”

storyBeats.text: You've been summoned to the Archmage's library. Towering shelves hold the Academy's design constitution — tokens that every spell in the kingdom must honour.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: Name by meaning, not by appearance. When the palette changes, code that speaks in meaning survives. Code that speaks in bg-blue-500 must be rewritten.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Assume the config extends colours so that bg-brand and text-brand-light are valid. Apply to the .card: bg-brand, text-brand-light, p-6, rounded-xl.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
The Arcane Order

Colours named by intent.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why is bg-brand better than bg-purple-700 at scale? What breaks if you spread colour-named classes across a 400-file codebase and then rebrand?

questions.questionHtml: Where do you define project-specific colours in Tailwind?
questions.explanationHtml: theme.extend.colors is the canonical place — it generates all matching utilities automatically.

questions.questionHtml: Which token layer should a reusable <Button> component reference directly?
questions.explanationHtml: Semantic tokens (brand, surface, danger) decouple components from raw palette values so rebrands and new themes stay cheap.

questions.questionHtml: A team spreads bg-purple-700 across 400 files. Marketing changes the brand colour. What's the fix, and what would have prevented it?
questions.correctAnswer: They must find-and-replace 400 files. A semantic token like bg-brand in theme.extend would have made it a one-line change.
questions.explanationHtml: Colour-named classes tie code to a palette. Semantic tokens tie code to intent — which is what actually persists across rebrands.

subChunks.title: Building a Design System
subChunks.hookHtml: Tokens are the vocabulary. A design system is the grammar — the components, variants, and patterns that make a thousand pages feel like one product.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The library doors open again. A second figure has joined Solomon at the workbench: a thin woman in a leather apron, sleeves rolled, chalk on her fingers. Solomon inclines his head.

Solomon: “This is Master Loras. She builds the components every team in the Academy uses.”

Master Loras: “A design system is not a folder of components. It is the set of decisions a team has already made so that no one has to re-decide them on Tuesday at 4pm. Let me show you the three tools you'll reach for in every real React codebase.”

1. clsx — conditional class strings.

import clsx from 'clsx';

<button className={clsx(
  'px-4 py-2 rounded font-medium',
  isActive && 'bg-brand text-white',
  disabled && 'opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed',
)}>

2. tailwind-merge — conflict resolution when classes collide.

import { twMerge } from 'tailwind-merge';

// Component defines px-4, but a caller passes px-8:
const className = twMerge('px-4 py-2', props.className);
// twMerge('px-4 px-8')  →  'px-8'    ✓ last wins, intelligently

3. class-variance-authority (CVA) — typed variants declared once.

import { cva, type VariantProps } from 'class-variance-authority';

const button = cva(
  'inline-flex items-center justify-center rounded font-medium transition',
  {
    variants: {
      intent: {
        primary: 'bg-brand text-white hover:bg-brand-dark',
        danger:  'bg-danger text-white hover:brightness-110',
        ghost:   'bg-transparent text-text hover:bg-surface',
      },
      size: {
        sm: 'px-3 py-1 text-sm',
        md: 'px-4 py-2',
        lg: 'px-6 py-3 text-lg',
      },
    },
    defaultVariants: { intent: 'primary', size: 'md' },
  }
);

<button className={button({ intent: 'danger', size: 'lg' })}>Delete</button>

Solomon: “Compose them. cva declares the variants, clsx layers in runtime conditions, twMerge resolves conflicts when callers override. This triad is the professional authoring layer for Tailwind in React.”

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: A design system is a compact between authors and users. Tokens are the treaty. Components are the enforcement.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Loras
storyBeats.text: Three tools: clsx for conditionals, twMerge for overrides, cva for variants. Learn the triad, stop re-deciding the same questions every sprint.

storyBeats.speaker: A typed button with CVA
storyBeats.text: const button = cva('rounded font-medium', { variants: { intent: { primary: 'bg-brand text-white' } } });

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Style a button that matches CVA's primary + md output. On .btn apply: bg-brand, text-white, rounded, font-medium, px-4, py-2, transition.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why does a team that accepts className props need tailwind-merge? Walk through what breaks without it when a caller passes px-8 to a component whose internal class string contains px-4.

options: Conflicts when class strings contain duplicate utilities from the same group
Generating dynamic class names at runtime
questions.correctAnswer: Conflicts when class strings contain duplicate utilities from the same group
questions.explanationHtml: twMerge understands Tailwind's utility groups and keeps the last winning class for each group.

questions.questionHtml: Which library gives you typed variants for a component (e.g. intent: 'primary' | 'danger') in one declaration?
questions.explanationHtml: CVA declares the entire variant lattice once and types itself through VariantProps.

questions.questionHtml: A team hand-rolls a <Dialog> component with focus-trap, escape-to-close, and ARIA roles. Six months later an accessibility audit fails on all of them. What should they have done instead?
questions.correctAnswer: Use Headless UI or Radix UI for the unstyled, accessible primitives, and style them with Tailwind — do not reinvent dialog/menu/combobox accessibility.
questions.explanationHtml: Accessible dialog, menu, and combobox primitives are hard and well-solved. Style Headless UI or Radix with Tailwind instead of re-implementing focus management and ARIA wiring from scratch.

subChunks.title: Accessibility in Depth
subChunks.hookHtml: Tailwind will happily let you ship an inaccessible interface. It's the author's job to choose classes that serve every reader — keyboard, screen-reader, low-vision, and reduced-motion users alike.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Solomon leads you down a spiral stair to a smaller room lit by a single lamp. A blindfolded scribe sits at the desk, tracing a page with her fingertips.

Solomon: “A spell that works for only some readers is a spell half-cast. Every utility you add is a choice about whose experience matters. Start with four habits and you will cover ninety percent of accessibility harm.”

Habit one: prefer focus-visible: over focus:.

// too loud — shows a ring on every mouse click
<button class="focus:ring-2 focus:ring-blue-500">

// just right — shows for keyboard users only
<button class="focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500">

Solomon: “focus: fires on every click. Mouse users see a ring they didn't ask for; designers hide it; keyboard users lose it too. focus-visible: only appears when the browser believes the focus came from the keyboard. Use it always.”

Habit two: contrast.

WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text. Tailwind's 50–300 shades rarely clear this on white.

Habit three: screen-reader-only text for icon-only controls.

<button aria-label="Close dialog">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" />
  <span class="sr-only">Close dialog</span>
</button>

Solomon: “sr-only removes the text from the screen without removing it from the accessibility tree.”

Habit four: respect prefers-reduced-motion.

<div class="motion-safe:animate-bounce motion-reduce:animate-none">
<div class="transition motion-reduce:transition-none">

ARIA variants. Tailwind ships aria-* variants so you can style from state without JavaScript class-toggling.

<button aria-expanded="false"
  class="bg-surface aria-expanded:bg-brand aria-expanded:text-white">
  Menu
</button>

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: A spell half-cast reaches half the readers. focus-visible:, contrast discipline, sr-only, and motion-reduce: — these are the spell, not its decoration.

storyBeats.speaker: Icon-only button that screen readers can still use

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Make the icon-only button accessible. On the .close-label span apply sr-only. On the .btn-close button apply focus-visible:ring-2 and focus-visible:ring-blue-500.

guidedPracticeTests.label: Button shows focus ring for keyboard

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why focus-visible: is a better default than focus: for interactive elements. What UX problem does focus: cause that focus-visible: solves?

options: Visually hides content but keeps it in the accessibility tree
Makes content visible only in print
questions.correctAnswer: Visually hides content but keeps it in the accessibility tree
questions.explanationHtml: sr-only uses CSS that is invisible on screen while still announced by screen readers.

questions.questionHtml: Which is the accessible minimum contrast ratio (WCAG AA) for body text?
questions.explanationHtml: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal-size body text; 3:1 for large text or UI chrome.

questions.questionHtml: motion-reduce: applies when the user has set prefers-reduced-motion.
questions.explanationHtml: motion-reduce: maps to the prefers-reduced-motion: reduce media query.

subChunks.title: Performance & Bundle Size
subChunks.hookHtml: Tailwind ships no CSS for classes you don't use — but only if your content globs are right. A misconfigured project can leak megabytes of unused CSS, or worse, silently drop styles that worked in dev.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Solomon climbs a ladder to the topmost shelf and pulls down a thin, well-thumbed volume titled simply The Scanner.

Solomon: “Tailwind's great virtue is that it emits nothing you do not use. Its great trap is that it decides what you use by reading your source files as text. If the scanner can't see a class string, that class does not exist.”

The content contract.

// tailwind.config.js
content: [
  './index.html',
  './src/**/*.{ts,tsx,jsx,vue,svelte}',
],

Solomon: “Forget a path and the styles from those files vanish from production. Too broad and the scanner walks node_modules and slows your builds. Be specific. Be complete.”

The dynamic-class trap.

// BAD — bg-${color}-500 never appears in source as a full string
const cls = `bg-${color}-500`;

// GOOD — full class strings exist for the scanner to find
const palette = {
  red:   'bg-red-500',
  blue:  'bg-blue-500',
  green: 'bg-green-500',
};
const cls = palette[color];

Solomon: “The symptom is always the same — works in dev, vanishes in production. Always write full class strings somewhere the scanner can read them.”

Safelist — for the truly dynamic.

// tailwind.config.js
safelist: [
  'bg-brand', 'text-white',
  { pattern: /bg-(red|blue|green)-(400|500|600)/ },
],

Purge and JIT. Modern Tailwind (v3+) runs JIT by default. The production build contains only the utilities you reference — typically 10–20 KB gzipped for a real app.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: The scanner reads your source as text. If it cannot see the full class name, the class does not exist. Every production bug in a Tailwind app eventually reduces to a variant of this one truth.

storyBeats.speaker: Safe dynamic class pattern
storyBeats.text: const palette = { red: 'bg-red-500', blue: 'bg-blue-500' }; const cls = palette[userChoice];

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Build a production-safe banner that uses only full, static class strings the JIT scanner can see. On the .banner apply: bg-brand, text-white, p-4, rounded-md, shadow-sm.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why bg-${color}-500 breaks Tailwind's JIT. How would you fix it without resorting to safelist?

questions.questionHtml: Where does Tailwind learn which classes to emit?
options: The content glob list in tailwind.config.js
Automatically, by scanning every file on disk
questions.correctAnswer: The content glob list in tailwind.config.js
questions.explanationHtml: The content array tells the JIT scanner which files to read for class names.

questions.questionHtml: Styles work in development but the production build is missing background colours generated via bg-${color}-500. What's the cause and cleanest fix?
questions.correctAnswer: The JIT scanner can't see interpolated class fragments. Replace with a static map like { red: 'bg-red-500', blue: 'bg-blue-500' } so full class strings appear in source.
questions.explanationHtml: The scanner uses plain string matching. Interpolation hides the full class name. Mapping to full strings is cleaner than safelist for known values.

subChunks.title: Large Application Architecture
subChunks.hookHtml: Utilities scale beautifully when you have a small app and three contributors. They rot quietly when you have fifty contributors, two hundred components, and no shared conventions. This chapter is the set of rules that keeps a Tailwind codebase readable after its first year.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
You return to the workbench. Master Loras has pinned a single sheet of parchment to the beam above it: The Archmage's Rules for Tailwind at Scale. Solomon reads them aloud, one by one.

Solomon: “These aren't style preferences. Each one is the residue of a real project that rotted when the rule was broken. Ignore them at your team's cost.”

Rule 1 — Components before @apply.

// AVOID — class abstraction in CSS
.btn-primary { @apply bg-brand text-white px-4 py-2 rounded; }

// PREFER — component abstraction in your framework
<Button intent="primary">Save</Button>

Rule 2 — Arbitrary values are a last resort.

// AVOID
<div class="mt-[17px] text-[#5A3D8C] w-[742px]">

// PREFER — extend theme, then use the utility
// tailwind.config.js: spacing: { '4.25': '17px' }, colors: { accent: '#5A3D8C' }
<div class="mt-4.25 text-accent">

Rule 3 — Order utilities consistently.

Adopt prettier-plugin-tailwindcss. It orders classes automatically by category. Reviewers stop arguing about class order; diffs become readable.

Rule 4 — One source of truth for each design decision.

  • Colours live in tailwind.config.js — never in inline styles.
  • Spacing scale lives in the config — never as arbitrary values in markup.
  • Typography ramp lives in the config — never duplicated as custom classes.

Rule 5 — Co-locate component CSS.

Tailwind classes live in the same file as the component that uses them.

Rule 6 — Enforce accessibility at the component boundary.

If <IconButton> exists, make aria-label a required prop.

Rule 7 — Document tokens, not components first.

Your design system's docs page should open with tokens: colour swatches, type scale, spacing ramp.

Loras: “Write cn on day one: twMerge(clsx(xs)). Use it everywhere. Your override story is now free.”

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: Seven rules. Each is the residue of a real codebase that rotted. Components before @apply. Arbitrary values sparingly. Consistent order. One source of truth. Co-locate. Enforce a11y at the boundary. Document tokens first.

storyBeats.speaker: Master Loras
storyBeats.text: Write cn on day one: twMerge(clsx(xs)). Use it everywhere. Your override story is now free.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Build a .btn-primary the component way — full utility classes on the element, no @apply and no arbitrary values. Apply: bg-brand, text-white, font-medium, px-4, py-2, rounded, hover:bg-brand-dark, focus-visible:ring-2.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: A teammate proposes defining every button in the app with @apply bg-brand text-white px-4 py-2 rounded. Make the case against it. What do you lose, and what should you do instead?

options: For unavoidable global targets (prose, form resets, third-party widgets you can't wrap)
As the default way to define component styles
To avoid long class strings in JSX
To keep CSS files feeling traditional
questions.correctAnswer: For unavoidable global targets (prose, form resets, third-party widgets you can't wrap)
questions.explanationHtml: For component abstraction, prefer actual components with CVA variants. Reserve @apply for places where a component wrapper isn't possible.

questions.questionHtml: Which tool automatically orders Tailwind classes in source files so reviewers stop arguing about diffs?
questions.explanationHtml: The official Prettier plugin reorders classes by category and keeps teams consistent without manual effort.

questions.questionHtml: A codebase is full of mt-[17px], w-[742px], text-[#5A3D8C]. What does this indicate, and what should the team do?
questions.correctAnswer: It's a sign the theme isn't keeping up with real design decisions. Extend the config (spacing, colors, typography) so those values become named tokens, and reserve arbitrary values for genuine one-offs.
questions.explanationHtml: Arbitrary values are an escape hatch. When they accumulate, the design system is being bypassed. Extending the theme re-centralises those decisions.

subChunks.title: Real-World Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: The final test of an archmage is not knowing utilities — it's assembling them into the handful of UI patterns every product ships: navigation, modals, dashboards, forms, tables. These are the shapes customers actually touch.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Solomon leads you out of the library and onto a balcony overlooking the Academy courtyard. From here you can see the Pattern Gardens — a collection of small living examples.

Solomon: “Five patterns will carry you through most products you ship. Learn them well and you can reason about any new screen as a composition of these shapes.”

1. Responsive navigation bar.

<nav class="flex items-center justify-between px-6 py-4 bg-surface shadow-sm">
  <a href="/" class="font-display text-xl text-brand">Arcana</a>
  <ul class="hidden md:flex items-center gap-6 text-sm">
    <li><a href="/topics" class="hover:text-brand">Topics</a></li>
  </ul>
  <button class="md:hidden p-2 rounded" aria-label="Open menu">☰</button>
</nav>

2. Sidebar + content shell.

<div class="min-h-screen grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-[240px_1fr]">
  <aside class="hidden md:block bg-surface border-r p-4"></aside>
  <main class="p-6"></main>
</div>

3. Modal / dialog.

<div class="fixed inset-0 bg-black/50 flex items-center justify-center p-4 z-50">
  <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true"
       class="w-full max-w-md bg-surface rounded-xl shadow-xl p-6">
    <h2 class="text-lg font-semibold">Confirm</h2>
    <div class="mt-6 flex justify-end gap-2">
      <button class="px-4 py-2 rounded bg-danger text-white">Delete</button>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

4. Card grid / dashboard stats.

<section class="grid grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4 gap-4">
  <div class="bg-surface rounded-xl p-6 shadow-sm">
    <p class="text-sm text-muted">Total XP</p>
    <p class="mt-2 text-3xl font-semibold">12,480</p>
  </div>
</section>

5. Responsive data table.

<table class="hidden md:table w-full text-sm"></table>
<ul class="md:hidden space-y-3"></ul>

Solomon: “Every product you ship is a recombination of these five shapes. You are no longer an apprentice.”

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: Five patterns: responsive nav, sidebar shell, modal, card grid, responsive table. Every product is a recombination of these shapes. Learn them and you can read any screen.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Build a stat card that fits inside a dashboard grid. On .stat apply: bg-surface, rounded-xl, p-6, shadow-sm, flex, flex-col, gap-2.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
Total XP

12,480
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Pick one pattern — nav, sidebar, modal, card grid, or responsive table. Explain the responsive decision it hinges on (which utility switches behaviour at which breakpoint, and why).

questions.questionHtml: Which pair of classes is idiomatic for a hamburger menu that appears only on small screens?
options: md:hidden on the button, hidden md:flex on the desktop menu
sm:block on the button, lg:hidden on the menu
questions.correctAnswer: md:hidden on the button, hidden md:flex on the desktop menu
questions.explanationHtml: Mobile-first: start hidden on the desktop menu, reveal with md:flex; start visible on the hamburger, hide with md:hidden.

questions.questionHtml: Which utility class creates the darkened, full-screen overlay behind a modal dialog?
questions.explanationHtml: fixed inset-0 pins to all four edges of the viewport; bg-black/50 is a 50%-opacity black overlay.

questions.questionHtml: A responsive dashboard ships with a <table> of user stats. On mobile it scrolls horizontally and users complain. What's the idiomatic Tailwind fix?
questions.correctAnswer: Render a <table class='hidden md:table'> for tablet and up, and a <ul class='md:hidden'> card list for mobile, backed by the same dataset.
questions.explanationHtml: Tables rarely collapse well. The two-view pattern — table on wide screens, cards on narrow — gives mobile users a native-feeling list without losing the desktop table.
